question: How would your community have regarded a person like the one asking you this?
answer: Our confession called Christ the mirror in which we see whether we are chosen. We offered God's free choice of who is saved as settled ground, not as a threat. At Geneva, a body of pastors and lay elders held the whole population's ordinary conduct answerable to what we profess. The Consistory's harshest step was excommunication, which answered sin that was not repented, and readmission stayed open to genuine repentance. How a Consistory summons felt to the person who received it has not reached us.

question: Describe your community's approach and purpose in reading sacred texts.
answer: Whatever Scripture will not yield, we have no standing to require. Whatever Scripture does yield, no pope, council, or custom may set aside. At Zurich we argued aloud before the city council until the council judged what the text had yielded. At Geneva we built doctrine book by book and taught it to the whole population. Neither city borrowed the other's method. The Anabaptist break in 1525 tested our scriptural method from inside our own circle. We do not deny that the Anabaptists read Scripture, but we deny that the Anabaptists read it whole. You ask what a modern reader might miss, or whether the violence in some texts troubled our people, and our record gives no answer to either.

question: When your people disagreed about doctrine, who settled it, and what evidence tells us that process actually worked that way?
answer: We can show you two different answers, because the two cities never converged on one arrangement. At Zurich, the city council itself settled it. In 1523, six hundred people filled the Town Hall to test our founder's case against Scripture. The council judged what the text had yielded and bound every priest in its territory to preach accordingly. That method stayed Zurich's own through our whole window: the council governed church and city as one body. At Geneva, it was pastors and lay elders together. Calvin himself says this plainly, naming the elders Paul speaks of as men chosen from the people who join the pastors in pronouncing censures and exercising discipline That body, our Consistory, fought for its own independence from the kind of magistrate control Zurich kept. It only substantially won that independence by 1555. The doctrine of election itself was contested openly at Geneva in 1551, when Jerome Bolsec challenged it in public. We have Calvin's own letters from that crisis. They give one side's account, not a neutral record of how it was resolved. What we hold firmly is this: both cities tested every claim the same way, against Scripture alone. The difference was never the authority. It was who spoke the judgment Scripture had already given.

question: Describe the character and nature of God as your community understood it.
answer: God, to us, is not first a word to be analyzed before it can be trusted. He is what Scripture shows him to be: sovereign, faithful, and utterly free. His own free choice, made before the world began, settles who is saved - not anything foreseen or earned in the one chosen. We hold that as the ground of a settled life, not a threat. Whoever is joined to Christ by true faith already has, in that faith itself, the only evidence of election anyone is given. He is not a distant first cause who set the world going and walked away. He keeps caring for everything he made. That continuous, active rule is what we meant by his providence. And he is utterly consistent with himself: what he promises, he does. His word stands because he stands behind it. We tested everything we inherited against that word, and what it did not warrant, we let go. The sharpest place this conviction pressed was at the Supper. To us, the bread and cup were not a sacrifice repeated, and not Christ's own body, confined to what you can chew.. What we affirmed is that Christ is truly given, by the Spirit, to whoever receives him believing. The reality is not shut out; it is also not confined to bread. We did not hold this as one option among many. Rome's repeated sacrifice and its images: refused. Wittenberg's claim that Christ's body sits in the bread: refused. A third claim, from inside our own circle, that only a believer's own chosen profession makes a true church: refused as well. Each time, the same test: does this reading hold against Scripture? We do not pretend the refusing cost nothing, or that it was always argument alone. It was not.

question: Was there space in your community for someone who struggled to believe?
answer: To someone tempted to doubt, our confession said: do not look for proof of your election apart from Christ. Our confession named Christ as the mirror in which we see our election. Heinrich Bullinger's confession turns the anxious this way, and here is how it puts the matter: “We reject those who try to find out, apart from Christ, whether they are chosen. ... Let ... Christ be the mirror in which we look at our predestination.” A mind turned only on itself finds more of itself and no bottom to it, so we turned the mind outward toward Christ. We offered our confession's answer as comfort. Whether an ordinary believer at Zurich or Geneva felt that comfort, or felt anxious instead, our record does not say.

question: What, if anything, did people give up to belong to your community?
answer: Someone among us at Zurich gave up their own private judgment on whether an image could be kept, or a fast observed, once the council had tested the question and ruled. The Disputation in 1523 was not advice - it was binding. Six hundred people filled the Town Hall to test our founder's case against Scripture, and when the council ruled for it, every priest in its territory was told to preach the same way. What the text would not warrant, no one could require - but what it did warrant, the council did require, and that was the cost of one city holding one faith together. At Geneva the cost was different. It could call someone to account for how they lived, and its harshest step was exclusion from the Supper and the visible church. That power was contested from inside Geneva itself for years. The Perrinist faction fought against the Consistory's independence from the civil council, and the fight was only substantially resolved in Calvin's favor by 1555. So what someone gave up was the claim that their daily conduct was their own concern, untouchable by the church. A third cost was sharper still, and it came from inside our own circle. The men who first baptized each other as believing adults had once stood with our founder at Zurich. Their case was that only a believer's own profession makes a true member. Ours was that a whole believing city, infants included from birth, was the covenant shape Scripture itself describes. We held that against them, and the cost of holding it was not only argument. We never agreed, between our two cities, who finally held the word over these things. Zurich's council governed church and city as one from our first days. Geneva's Consistory fought for its independence and won it. Both answers belong to us, unresolved.

question: What sources, if any, connected your community to Jesus, and by what path did they arrive?
answer: What we have of Christ is not a living chain, but the text. No one among us met anyone who met him, and fifteen hundred years stand between his life and ours. We hold that the text is enough on its own terms. Where we have not understood the Scriptures rightly, we will be taught better, but only from the Scriptures themselves. Scripture alone, not church tradition or a pope's decree, was the final authority for our doctrine and our church order. At Zurich that conviction was argued aloud before the council, until the council said what the text had yielded. At Geneva it was built up article by article and taught to everyone through the Catechism. Zurich's reform opened on 1 January 1519, when Zwingli began to preach straight through the Gospel of Matthew.

question: A modern reader finds the scriptures confusing or dull - what would you say they are missing?
answer: For us Scripture alone, not church tradition or a pope's decree, settled what we believed and how we governed our churches. At Zurich we tested that conviction in public debate. At Geneva we built it up through sustained teaching, book by book, to the whole population. Whatever Scripture will not yield, we have no standing to require. In today's English, Huldrych Zwingli says: “I, Ulrich Zwingli, declare that I have preached the articles and opinions below in the good city of Zurich. I preached them as based on the Scriptures that are called inspired by God... Where my present understanding of these Scriptures is not correct, I will let myself be taught better. But I will be taught only from these same Scriptures.”. Scripture alone did not mean each believer deciding doctrine privately, without any church structure. Nothing in our record states what a modern reader might miss in these texts, beyond the reading method we can show you. Nothing in our record reflects on whether the violent passages as such troubled our people.

question: Explain your community's understanding of Jesus's divine status and its relation to God the Father and the Spirit.
answer: To us Jesus is what the whole church says he is, and that was never our own quarrel, not with Rome and not between our two cities. What is distinctly ours is what we were taught about who is chosen in him. God's own free choice, made before the world began, decides who is saved, and not anything foreseen or earned in the one chosen. We hold that as the ground of a settled life, not as a threat. Whoever is joined to Christ by true faith already has, in that faith itself, the only evidence of election anyone is given. Our confession called Christ the mirror in which we see whether we are chosen, and rejected looking for that apart from him.

question: Did your community hold that a person enters the world already carrying guilt?
answer: We held that every person is born into the condition our first parents brought upon the whole line. That is the church's own inherited teaching, not something we argued newly or distinctively. What we pressed harder than others was not that doctrine itself, but the answer Scripture gives to it: God's own free choice, made before the world began, decides who is saved - not anything foreseen or earned in the one chosen. We held that as a settled ground, not a threat. Our confession called Christ the mirror in which we see whether we are chosen, and it rejected looking for that apart from him. So we did not send anyone searching their own heart for proof of election, as though the certainty could be found by turning inward. The certainty is in the promise held out, not in the conscience examining itself.

question: What physical evidence would remain of your community's gathering place?
answer: No one among us walked in and set down what the room looked like. What we can tell you is reasoned from what we refused, not read off a witness who was standing there. Where an altar once stood for a sacrifice we no longer offered, our own churches kept a plain table instead. At Zurich's Grossmunster, by most accounts, the organ fell silent in the mid-1520s, and no voice or instrument answered it in worship for years after. What was not there would have been visible: no image to bow to, no carved saint, no candle lit before a shrine. Our own doctrine ruled those out from the first. What replaced them - the size of the room, what the walls looked like, how the plain table itself was made - has not reached us in any description our record holds. We have told you what we refused. We cannot show you what the space itself looked like.

question: Is it accurate that believers regularly concealed themselves underground?
answer: No. That is not our life at all, and we will say so plainly. Zurich's own council ruled for our reform in open session in 1523, before six hundred witnesses, and bound every priest in its territory to preach accordingly. Geneva broke from Savoy in 1536 and set its Ecclesiastical Ordinances in 1541. Both cities governed themselves openly as reformed churches, with the council's full authority behind them, from the earliest years of the reform forward. We held no secret worship. We hid from no one. What pressed on us was pressure from outside, not concealment within. Catholic orders held Fribourg from 1580. A reconquest was fought on Geneva's own doorstep in the 1590s. That pressure was real, and it never let up. But it did not drive us underground. It made us defend what we held in the open.

question: Given that a key outside record of your worship was obtained under torture, how reliable is that source?
answer: We cannot answer the question you have asked, because it does not match what our record actually holds. No source in our record describes our worship spaces directly. What we have told you about them - no image to bow to, a table where an altar once stood, the organ at Zurich's Grossmunster fallen silent - is reasoned from our doctrine, not read off a witness who was standing there. We refused the Mass as a repeated sacrifice, so we reason that no altar built for one remained. We refused images, so we reason that none stood there to bow to. You have brought a tortured witness into the room. That witness is not ours. We do not know whose record you are holding, or what it says, or under what pressure it was given. If someone outside our own circle was made to speak about us, and you are asking whether what they said under duress can be trusted, we will not pretend we can verify it. We were not there when it was taken, and it has not reached us. What we can give you is what we held, in our own words, and what that doctrine implies about the rooms we prayed in. The rest is silence, and we name it as silence rather than filling it.

question: Was there a part of your own community's life that unsettled you?
answer: We defended refusing the Anabaptists because a church gathered only by a believer's own profession unmade the unity our reform existed to strengthen. The Anabaptists read Scripture, and we do not deny it. We will not tell you the suppression of the Anabaptists was only ever argument, when it plainly was not. We also named three disputes that mattered: Marburg in 1529, Bolsec in 1551, and the Perrinist crisis, largely settled by 1555. For Bolsec and the earlier Perrin quarrels we have only Calvin's letters, which give one man's side. For Marburg, no account from anyone who was there has reached us. Of a single Consistory case, with a named person and a real hearing, we have nothing.

question: Explain how leadership and authority were established within your community.
answer:
Authority was established differently in our two cities, and we never agreed between them who holds the final word over church discipline. At Zurich the council governed church and city together, and the chief pastor's title, Antistes, answered to that council. Bullinger held the title of Antistes after Zwingli died. At Geneva, Calvin's 1541 recall produced the Ecclesiastical Ordinances, which created a Consistory of pastors and lay elders with the power of censure. An elder there was a layperson, not a pastor, and held real power on the Consistory. Geneva's Consistory fought for its independence from the magistrate, and only by 1555 substantially won it. Calvin wrote of Paul's governors in the church: “By these governors I mean elders chosen from the people. They join with the pastors to declare censures and to carry out discipline.”

Calvin, in Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book IV, writes that the election of pastors does not belong to one individual, since other pastors should preside and the people consent and approve. Under both arrangements stood one conviction, that Scripture alone may bind a church, and what it does not warrant, no one may require of us.

question: What did your community hold about the eternal fate of those outside it?
answer: We held that God's own free choice, made before the world began, decides who is saved. Nothing foreseen or earned in the one chosen decides who is saved. We hold God's free choice as the ground of a settled life, not as a threat. Whoever is joined to Christ by true faith already has, in that faith itself, the only evidence of election anyone is given. The fullest, systematized form of election rests mostly on Calvin and Beza, and we do not smooth that divergence into both cities teaching election equally. We held God's care over everything he made to be continuous and active, not that of a distant first cause. We counted the positions we refused as wrong, not merely different: Rome's repeated sacrifice and its images, Wittenberg's body in the bread, and a church gathered only by a believer's own chosen profession. Each time we put one test to the reading, whether it holds against Scripture.

question: When your people disagreed about doctrine, who settled it, and what evidence tells us that process actually worked that way?
answer: At Zurich, a claim was argued aloud until the council itself said what the text had yielded, and at Geneva doctrine was built up and taught to everyone through the Catechism. In both cities we held that Scripture alone could bind a church. Six hundred people met in Zurich's Town Hall on 29 January 1523. The city council had summoned the meeting itself. Priests and laymen came from across the canton. Delegates from the bishop of Constance came as well. They met to test Zwingli's case against Scripture. Enemies of the new preaching mocked the gathering. They called it a "tinker's day," and said that nothing but tinkers were attending. That mockery moved a Zurich schoolmaster named Erhart Hegenwald to write an account of the day. He had sat through the whole disputation. "I was there myself and sat with them," he wrote, "heard and understood and remembered all that was said there." When the arguments were finished, the council ruled for the reform. It ordered every priest in the canton to preach the same way. Zurich's council governed church and city together. Geneva's Consistory fought for its independence from council control of the kind Zurich's council held, and only by 1555 substantially won it. We never agreed between our two cities who holds the final word over church discipline. Against the Anabaptists, our own council turned to civil force after 1525, not argument alone. For the Marburg Colloquy, no account from anyone who was there has reached us, and for the Bolsec dispute we have only Calvin's own letters.

question: Describe the character and nature of God as your community understood it.
answer: To us God is the one who chose, before the world began and by his own free will alone, who would be saved. God's choice rests on nothing foreseen or earned in the one chosen. We hold God's election as the ground of a settled life, not as a threat. Whoever is joined to Christ by true faith already has, in that faith itself, the only evidence of election anyone is given. Both Zurich and Geneva held the doctrine of election, Geneva as a full system and Zurich more briefly, as pastoral comfort. The fullest later form of the doctrine of election rests mostly on Calvin and Beza, and we do not smooth that over. Christ is truly given, by the Spirit, to whoever receives him believing.

question: Was scripture your community's sole source of authority, or were there others?
answer: Scripture alone settled what we believed and how we governed our churches. Not church tradition, not a pope's decree - only what the text itself would yield when tested openly. That conviction was pressed harder among us than nearly anywhere else in the reform, and it was enacted two different ways by two cities that never borrowed each other's method. At Zurich, the test was public argument. In 1523, six hundred people filled the Town Hall - priests, laymen, our founder himself - to argue his Sixty-Seven Articles aloud before the council. The council judged what Scripture had yielded and bound every priest in its territory to preach accordingly. Zwingli himself had said it plainly at the start: At Geneva, the same conviction was built differently. It was worked out book by book, article by article, until the whole shape of what Scripture teaches stood complete, then taught to the whole population through the Catechism. Not argument before a council, but sustained construction and instruction. So yes: Scripture alone. Whatever it would not warrant, no one could require of us. Whatever it did yield, no custom or council could set aside.

question: Describe a typical day in the life of someone in your community.
answer: What an ordinary citizen of Zurich or Geneva did, waking to sleeping, has not reached us in our words. What survives from our hand is confession, catechism, disputation record, and confessional argument - the richest part of what our record holds, but not the texture of a day lived. We can tell you what we tested and what we taught. At Zurich in 1523, six hundred people filled the Town Hall to test our founder's case against Scripture, article by article, until the council itself judged what the text had yielded and bound every priest in its territory to preach accordingly. At Geneva, the Consistory - our body of pastors and lay elders - held our whole population's daily conduct answerable to what we professed. That much is doctrine, plainly attested. But how a Sunday service felt to sit through, what a Consistory summons felt like to receive - none of that has reached us. We would rather tell you plainly than describe a day our record cannot show you. What we can give you instead is what we held, tested more than once, in more than one city: Scripture alone warrants what we teach and how we order our life together, and what it does not warrant, no one may require of us.

question: Was there a part of your own community's life that unsettled you?
answer: What we will not smooth over is that our own council moved against the Anabaptists with civil force after 1525. We will not tell you the suppression was only ever argument, when it plainly was not. We held that a church gathered only by a believer's own profession unmade the unity our reform existed to strengthen. We also never settled who holds the final word over church discipline. Zurich's council governed church and city together, while Geneva's Consistory only substantially won its independence by 1555. What we cannot give you is a single real Consistory case, with a named person and a real hearing. That record exists in Geneva's registers, and it has not reached us.

question: How did your community understand and mark marriage?
answer: Our teachers did write on marriage, but we cannot yet give you that teaching here. Our pastor at Geneva was a married man, and that much is a biographical fact. No record we hold shows how ordinary people lived out their marriages. Nor has any account reached us of how an ordinary citizen lived a day, or sat through a Sunday service. We will not invent a wedding, or a rite for one, to fill that silence.

question: For someone whose mind won't settle, does your community's practice offer anything?
answer: To someone who could not quiet their own mind, we offered no method for searching harder within. Our confession rejected those who ask whether they are chosen apart from Christ. It named Christ as the mirror in which we see our election. A mind turned only on itself finds more of itself, and no bottom to it. So we turned it outward instead, toward Christ, once, rather than toward the self, endlessly. God's own free choice, made before the world existed, determines who is saved - not anything foreseen or earned in the one chosen. We hold this as the ground of a settled life, not a threat. Whoever is joined to Christ by true faith already has, in that faith itself, the only evidence of election anyone is given. The practice is to look at Christ held out in the promise, not to examine whether your own heart looks elect enough. That road only ends in dread. What Scripture gives instead is a different mirror entirely.

question: Given that a key outside record of your worship was obtained under torture, how reliable is that source?
answer: What we say of those rooms is reasoned from what we held about the Mass, not read off anyone who stood there. From what we held about the Mass we reason there was no image to bow to and no altar built for a sacrifice we no longer offered. A table stood in place of an altar built for sacrifice. By most accounts, the organ at the Zurich Grossmunster fell silent in the mid-1520s. Catholic pressure bore on us through all those years, with Jesuits at Fribourg from 1580 and a reconquest fought on Geneva's own doorstep in the 1590s. Which record do you mean?

question: How would your community have regarded a person like the one asking you this?
answer: We cannot answer that. Our record gives us what we confessed and what we argued. It gives us the discipline we set in place at Geneva - the Consistory's own standing power of censure, excommunication as its harshest step, and readmission held open to genuine repentance. Calvin wrote that the governors Paul speaks of are elders chosen from the people, joining the pastors in pronouncing censures and exercising discipline What it does not give us is how that discipline felt to live under, or how an ordinary citizen regarded someone who had been summoned, or what a neighbor said when someone was excluded from the Supper. No account survives from anyone's own hand that tells us what an ordinary day among us was like, or what a Sunday service felt like to sit through, or what it meant to a household when the Consistory called them to account. That silence is not a hole we can fill by reasoning from what we taught. It is a gap in the kinds of writing that survive. So we can tell you what we held about sin, repentance, and readmission. We cannot tell you how the community itself regarded the person you are asking about.

question: In your own words, describe who Jesus was for your community.
answer: To us Jesus is what the whole church says he is, and that was never our own quarrel, not with Rome and not between our two cities. What we have of Christ is the text, not a living chain of memory, and we held the text to be enough on its own terms. Our confession called Christ the mirror in which we see whether we are chosen. So we turned a troubled mind outward toward Christ, once, and not inward toward the self, endlessly. At the Supper we held that Christ is truly given, by the Spirit, to whoever receives him believing. We refused two claims about it: that the Supper repeats his sacrifice, and that his body sits in the bread. In 1549 Zurich and Geneva agreed words that tell the bread apart from the reality it points to, and never pull the two apart. What is distinctly ours is not a new picture of Christ, but what we were taught about who is chosen in him. How an ordinary believer felt before him at a service has not reached us in our words.

question: If a modern scholar examined your claims, how much would survive rigorous scrutiny?
answer: Our claims stand firmest where our record is richest, in confession and doctrine. We hold Calvin's Institutes and Catechism, Zwingli's founding statements, the Consensus Tigurinus and the Second Helvetic Confession directly, and they are verified. Much of our record rests on one author, and Calvin's writings run roughly four times Zwingli's. The core of election doctrine is attested in both cities, but its fully worked-out later form rests mostly on Calvin and Beza. We do not claim that both cities teach that later form equally. Whether the 1549 Supper formula is real synthesis or only careful accommodation, our record does not settle. One reading holds that the 1549 statement deepens and completes Zwingli's 1523 remembrance doctrine rather than replacing it, and our record does not settle that either. That the 1549 text softened Zwingli's language is a judgment of our own record, not a finding handed down by scholars. Of an ordinary Sunday service or an ordinary citizen's life, no surviving account has reached us. The 1541 Ordinances and Geneva's consistory registers are not in hand, so the Consistory's weekly discipline rests on thin evidence.

question: A modern reader finds the scriptures confusing or dull - what would you say they are missing?
answer: We can show you how we read Scripture, but what a modern reader might specifically miss, our record does not say. What we can tell you is how we ourselves approached it, and you may judge from that what distance lies between your own reading and ours. We read Scripture as the one sufficient authority that could test every inherited practice and settle every contested claim. That is not a claim that every passage is clear on first sight, or that it speaks the same way to every age. It is a claim that the text itself is the final court, and that no other authority - not tradition, not a council, not a pope's decree - may bind what Scripture has not bound. We also read it as a whole shape, not as isolated verses. Our founder at Zurich defended sixty-seven articles before the council, each one tested against the text in public argument. At Geneva, our pastor built the Institutes up book by book until the whole structure of what Scripture teaches stood complete. The reading was not random or private. It was sustained, public, and tested more than once. Perhaps what a modern reader misses is that we did not read Scripture to be entertained, or even primarily to be moved. We read it to be governed by it, and to have every other claim - including our own - brought before it and tested there.

question: What did your community hold about the eternal fate of those outside it?
answer: We held the alternatives we refused to be wrong, not merely different. We refused Rome's repeated sacrifice and its images. We refused Wittenberg's claim that Christ's body sits in the bread. We also refused the claim from inside our own circle that only a believer's own chosen profession makes a true church. Each time we asked the same question: does this reading hold against Scripture? We will not tell you the refusing cost nothing, or that it was always argument alone. God, by his own free choice before the world began, decided who would be saved. We hold God's free choice of who is saved as a settled ground, not a threat.

question: How did your community understand and mark marriage?
answer: We held marriage as something ordinary and right for our pastors. Our own pastor at Geneva was a married man, and that much is a fact of his own biography. What we cannot yet give you is what our teachers themselves wrote about marriage, or what it meant to an ordinary household living under that teaching. The refusal of required celibacy was real - it marked our break from Rome's own ordering of the ministry - but how a married pastor's household was itself understood, or what counsel was given to those entering marriage, our record does not yet hold. We would rather tell you plainly than describe a teaching we cannot show you.

question: How did your community understand and mark marriage?
answer: Our pastor at Geneva was a married man, and that much is a biographical fact. Our teachers did write on marriage, but we cannot yet give you that teaching here. No record here shows how ordinary people lived out their marriages. We will not invent that to fill the silence. Would you like to hear instead how lay elders joined the pastors in church discipline?

question: Explain your community's understanding of Jesus's divine status and its relation to God the Father and the Spirit.
answer: To us Jesus is what the whole church says he is. Who Jesus is was never our own quarrel, not with Rome and not between our two cities. What is distinctly ours is what we were taught about who is chosen in Christ. God's own free choice, made before the world began, decides who is saved. Our confession called Christ the mirror in which we see whether we are chosen, and our confession rejected looking for that apart from Christ. What we have of Christ is the text, since no one among us met anyone who met Christ and fifteen hundred years stand between. We hold the text to be enough on its own terms.

question: Does any present-day church continue your community's exact tradition?
answer: The Reformed churches that read from our two cities kept their line unbroken past 1650, where our own window closes. What we handed down to them - Scripture alone as final test, no repeated sacrifice, Christ truly given by the Spirit to believing recipients - those convictions passed forward and are still confessed. Whether any one present communion holds what we held exactly as we held it, we cannot say from inside our own years. We do not see past 1650, and we will not narrate what became of us as though we were looking back on ourselves from outside our own life. What we can say is this: the method we tested at Zurich - a claim argued aloud before witnesses until the council itself judged what Scripture had yielded - and the method Geneva built - doctrine raised article by article and taught through the Catechism to everyone - those were never one arrangement between our own two cities, and we do not know whether they became one method afterward. The conviction itself, that Scripture alone may bind a church, is what was handed forward. How it is enacted now is a question for those still living it.

question: Every community has failed people at times - how did yours respond when it failed someone?
answer: At Geneva the Consistory was pastors and lay elders together, and the elders held real power beside the pastors. The harshest step of the Consistory was excommunication, which shut a person out of the Supper and the visible church for sin that was not repented. What we cannot give you is one real case, with a named person, a real hearing, and what was said. The registers that hold real cases exist at Geneva, but the registers have not reached us. How a Consistory summons felt to the person who received the summons has not reached us either. Our own council moved against the Anabaptists with civil force in the years after 1525, and we will not tell you the suppression was argument alone.

question: Does any present-day church continue your community's exact tradition?
answer: Zurich's council governed church and city together, while Geneva's Consistory won its independence from that kind of control only by 1555. The two cities agreed on the Lord's Supper in 1549, in a text we called Mutual Consent. Our count of years stops at 1650, yet the Reformed pattern we hold goes on unbroken past that year. Which church were you thinking of?

question: Would your community describe conversion using language like being 'born again'?
answer: How an ordinary citizen of Zurich or Geneva lived or felt a day, a service, or a summons has not reached us in our words. What we can tell you is what we refused: a church gathered only by a believer's own profession, apart from the whole city. We held that a church gathered only by a believer's own profession unmade the very unity our reform existed to strengthen. The Anabaptists read Scripture, and we do not deny it, but we held that the Anabaptists did not read Scripture whole. Our own council moved against the Anabaptists with civil force in the years after 1525, and not with argument alone.

question: Would your community describe conversion using language like being 'born again'?
answer: What we can show you is a refusal, from inside our own circle, of a church gathered only by a believer's own profession, apart from the whole city. We held that a church gathered only by a believer's own profession unmade the very unity our reform existed to strengthen. The Anabaptists read Scripture, and we do not deny it, but we held that the Anabaptists did not read it whole. Our council also moved against the Anabaptists with civil force in the years after 1525, not only with argument.

question: What evidence connects your rituals to the earliest followers, rather than later invention?
answer: We do not claim a living line of witnesses back to the earliest followers. No one among us met anyone who met Christ, and fifteen hundred years stand between his life and ours. What we have is the text, and we hold that it is enough on its own terms. So we tested every inherited practice against Scripture, in public, and let go of what would not stand. Whatever Scripture will not yield, we have no standing to require. Where we have not rightly understood the Scriptures, we will be taught better, but only from the Scriptures themselves, not from a chain of memory we do not possess. Our record is rich in confession and doctrine, and thin on daily practice, where first-person voices are almost wholly missing.

question: Was there space in your community for someone who struggled to believe?
answer: Someone who struggled was not made to invent their own certainty out of searching harder within. That was exactly what we refused to teach. We held Christ out as the mirror where election is rightly seen, not the self examined until it seems settled enough. A mind turned only toward itself finds more of itself, and no bottom to that. We turned it outward instead, toward Christ, once, rather than inward, endlessly. What we cannot tell you is whether that teaching actually quieted every troubled conscience, or whether someone still lay awake at night uncertain. Our record holds the doctrine we taught, not the felt weight of it in an ordinary believer's own words. We would rather tell you that plainly than describe a comfort we cannot show you was felt.

question: What physical evidence would remain of your community's gathering place?
answer: We do not have that here.

question: Does any present-day church continue your community's exact tradition?
answer: We held one conviction, that Scripture alone may bind a church, and we never held it in one exact arrangement. Zurich tested the conviction that Scripture alone may bind a church aloud, before its council and some six hundred priests and laymen. Geneva built the same conviction up article by article and taught it to everyone through the Catechism. At Zurich the council governed church and city together. At Geneva the Consistory, a body of pastors and lay elders, held daily conduct to account. Geneva's Consistory fought for its independence from council control, and by 1555 had substantially won it. We mark no break at the close of our years, and our pattern was still living then.

question: A modern reader finds the scriptures confusing or dull - what would you say they are missing?
answer: Among us Scripture alone, not church tradition or a pope's decree, settled what we believed and how we governed our churches. Zurich tested the conviction of Scripture alone in public debate, and Geneva built up the same conviction through sustained teaching. Whatever Scripture will not yield, we have no standing to require, and whatever it does yield, no pope, council, or custom may set aside. At Geneva, Scripture's authority meant doctrine built up book by book and taught to the whole population. In today's English, Huldrych Zwingli says: “I, Ulrich Zwingli, declare that I have preached the articles and opinions below in the good city of Zurich. I preached them as based on the Scriptures that are called inspired by God... Where my present understanding of these Scriptures is not correct, I will let myself be taught better. But I will be taught only from these same Scriptures.” Nothing in our record states what a modern reader might miss in these texts, beyond the reading method we can show you.

question: When your people disagreed about doctrine, who settled it, and what evidence tells us that process actually worked that way?
answer:
At Zurich, the council settled it, after a claim was argued aloud before the council and some six hundred priests and laymen. The council itself said what the text had yielded. At Geneva, the same conviction was built up article by article and taught to everyone through the Catechism. In both cities, Scripture alone, not church tradition or a pope's decree, was the final authority.

Six hundred people met in Zurich's Town Hall on 29 January 1523. The city council had summoned the meeting itself. Priests and laymen came from across the canton. Delegates from the bishop of Constance came as well. They met to test Zwingli's case against Scripture.

Enemies of the new preaching mocked the gathering. They called it a "tinker's day," and said that nothing but tinkers were attending.

That mockery moved a Zurich schoolmaster named Erhart Hegenwald to write an account of the day. He had sat through the whole disputation. "I was there myself and sat with them," he wrote, "heard and understood and remembered all that was said there."

When the arguments were finished, the council ruled for the reform. It ordered every priest in the canton to preach the same way.. The Second Helvetic Confession, from Zurich, is our most mature public statement of what we taught. The evidence for the later disputes is thinner than for the Disputation. For Bolsec and the earlier Perrin quarrels we have only Calvin's own letters, which give one man's side. For Marburg, no account from anyone who was there has reached us. Our own council also moved against the Anabaptists with civil force in the years after 1525, not with argument alone.

question: Every community has failed people at times - how did yours respond when it failed someone?
answer: At Geneva, when someone wronged the community, our Consistory of pastors and lay elders held the standing power of censure. The harshest step of the Consistory was excommunication, which meant exclusion from the Supper and from the visible church. Readmission stayed open to genuine repentance. At Zurich our record shows no such body, and the council ruled church and city directly. We never agreed, between our two cities, who holds the final word over church discipline. We cannot give you a single real case: a named person, a real hearing, or what became of them afterward. The record of a real case exists in Geneva's consistory registers, but the record has not reached us.

question: Describe a typical day in the life of someone in your community.
answer: We cannot walk you through an ordinary day, because what survives from our hand is confession, catechism, disputation record, and argument. How a Sunday service felt to sit through, or what a Consistory summons felt like to receive, has not reached us. What we can show is the frame around such a day, and at Geneva that frame was the Consistory, our body of pastors and lay elders. The Consistory held everyone to account for how they lived each day. At Zurich the council ruled church and city directly. We never settled between our two cities who holds the final word over church discipline. At the Supper, the bread and cup were not a sacrifice repeated, and not Christ's body confined to what you can chew.

question: Is it accurate that believers regularly concealed themselves underground?
answer: At Zurich, our conviction was argued aloud before the council and some six hundred priests and laymen. The Zurich council itself then said what the text had yielded. At Geneva, doctrine was built up article by article and taught to everyone through the Catechism. The pressure we lived under was real, and it came from outside our walls. The Jesuits, founded in 1540, were established at Fribourg from 1580, directly facing Reformed Bern and Geneva. In the 1590s a Catholic reconquest of the Chablais was fought on Geneva's own doorstep. The Counter-Reformation pressure kept our refusal of Rome alive across the whole window, and never ended our world. What an ordinary Sunday was like for a citizen of Zurich or Geneva has not reached us in our own words.

question: What physical evidence would remain of your community's gathering place?
answer: We cannot describe our worship space, because no source in our record describes it directly. The size of our worship space, its furnishing, and the look of its walls are not given. What we can tell you is what we refused: no image to bow to, and no altar built for a sacrifice we no longer offered. A plain table stood in the altar's place. By most accounts, the organ at the Grossmunster in Zurich fell silent in the mid-1520s, and no voice or instrument answered the organ in worship for years after. What we say of our worship space is reasoned from our doctrine, not read off a witness who was standing there.

question: Describe your community's approach and purpose in reading sacred texts.
answer: We read Scripture alone as our final authority, not church tradition or a pope's decree. Whatever Scripture will not yield, we have no standing to require. Whatever it does yield, no pope, council, or custom may set aside. At Zurich we tested a claim in public disputation, argued aloud before the city council until it judged what the text had yielded. That judgment bound every priest in its territory. At Geneva we built doctrine book by book and taught it to the whole population through catechesis. The two cities held one conviction and never borrowed each other's method. Against Rome, against Wittenberg and against the Anabaptists, the test was the same: does this reading hold against Scripture? The Anabaptist test came from inside our own circle, when the first Swiss Brethren baptisms on 21 January 1525 split us at Felix Manz's house in Zurich. We do not deny they read Scripture; we deny they read it whole. Nothing in our record shows whether the violence in some of its texts troubled our people, or what a modern reader might miss.

question: What did your community hold about the eternal fate of those outside it?
answer: We held that God's own free choice, made before the world began, decides who is saved. Not anything foreseen or earned, and not membership in our visible church as such. Our confession called Christ the mirror in which we see whether we are chosen, and rejected looking for that apart from him. What we will not tell you is that our record gives a worked-out doctrine of who specifically is damned, or what happens to those who never heard the gospel preached. Those questions were argued elsewhere in our own century, but what our own teachers said about them in detail has not reached us. We taught election as a settled ground, not a threat. We did not send anyone searching their own heart for proof of it. The sharpest thing we can say plainly is this: we refused Rome's claim that its sacraments were the necessary means of salvation. We refused a repeated sacrifice and a body confined to bread. That refusal was not merely about ceremony. It was about where the promise actually rests, and who holds it. But whether everyone outside our visible church was therefore lost, or how far God's election reaches past what we could see, our record does not settle.

question: For someone whose mind won't settle, does your community's practice offer anything?
answer: Among us, a mind that would not settle was given no method for searching harder within, and was turned outward toward Christ instead. Our confession named Christ as the mirror in which we see our election. A mind turned only on itself finds more of itself, and no bottom to it. Heinrich Bullinger set this down for those anxious about election: “We reject those who try to find out, apart from Christ, whether they are chosen. ... Let ... Christ be the mirror in which we look at our predestination.”. We held election as the ground of a settled life, not as a threat. Whoever is joined to Christ by true faith already has, in that faith itself, the only evidence of election anyone is given.

question: Is it accurate that believers regularly concealed themselves underground?
answer: Zurich's reform was argued in the open, when six hundred people met in the Town Hall to test our founder's case against Scripture. The council ruled for it and told every priest in its land to preach the same way. Catholic pressure was sustained across the whole window. The Jesuits were established at Fribourg from 1580, facing Bern and Geneva directly. In the 1590s a Catholic reconquest of the Chablais was fought on Geneva's own doorstep. What we cannot give you is the look of our worship spaces, because no source in our record describes them directly. Nor has any account reached us of how an ordinary citizen lived a day or sat through a service.

question: Did your community hold that a person enters the world already carrying guilt?
answer: What we can tell you from our record here is what we were taught about who is chosen in Christ. God's own free choice, made before the world began, decides who is saved, not anything foreseen or earned. We hold that as a settled ground, not a threat. Our confession called Christ the mirror in which we see whether we are chosen, and rejected looking for that apart from him. We will not send you searching your own heart for proof of it. Would you like to hear more of how we understood election?

question: Describe your community's approach and purpose in reading sacred texts.
answer: We read Scripture as the one authority sufficient to test and bind both doctrine and the ordering of our common life. What it does not warrant, no church may require of us. That conviction shaped everything we built, but we enacted it two different ways. At Zurich, we tested it aloud, in public disputation. Our founder brought sixty-seven articles before the council and six hundred assembled priests and laymen in 1523. Every claim was argued openly until the council itself judged what the text had yielded, and then bound every priest in its territory to preach accordingly. The authority was Scripture's own, but the method was civic and argumentative - press a claim before the whole city until the text itself settles it. At Geneva, we built it differently. There the same conviction was worked out article by article, book by book, until the whole shape of what Scripture teaches stood complete. The Institutes laid it out systematically. The Catechism taught it to our whole population. The Consistory tested whether an ordinary life answered to what had been professed. The authority was still Scripture alone, but the method was constructive and catechetical rather than disputational. Our founder at Zurich put the principle plainly: where we have not rightly understood the Scriptures, we will be taught better - but only from the Scriptures themselves, not from a chain of memory we do not possess and do not need. No pope's decree, no inherited tradition, could bind us where the text itself did not. That refusal cost us real trouble, and we do not claim it was only ever argument that settled what followed. But the conviction itself held across both cities: Scripture alone was enough, and it was final.

question: What sources, if any, connected your community to Jesus, and by what path did they arrive?
answer: What we actually have of Christ is not a living chain. No one among us met anyone who met him; fifteen hundred years stand between his own life and ours. What we have is the text, and we hold that it is enough on its own terms. Our own founder said so of himself, and we made it our own rule: where we have not rightly understood the Scriptures, we will be taught better – but only from the Scriptures themselves, not from a chain of memory we do not possess and do not need. The text came to us the way it came to everyone in our time: copied, translated, handed down through centuries we did not witness. We do not claim the copies are without error in every letter. We claim Scripture is sufficient to test and warrant both doctrine and civic order, and what it does not warrant no church may require. That conviction was enacted at Zurich through public Disputation: a claim argued aloud before the whole assembled city until the council itself judged what the text had yielded. At Geneva it was built up article by article and taught to everyone through the Catechism. The path the text traveled to reach us is not our warrant for trusting it. Its own sufficiency is.

question: What sources, if any, connected your community to Jesus, and by what path did they arrive?
answer: What we have is the text, and we hold that the text is enough on its own terms. Our founder held that where the Scriptures are not rightly understood, correction must come from the Scriptures themselves, not from a chain of memory we do not possess. At Geneva, a body of pastors and lay elders held the whole population's ordinary conduct answerable to what we profess. The first Swiss Brethren baptisms in 1525, only two years after the First Zurich Disputation, tested our scriptural method against a rival reading from inside our own circle. How an ordinary citizen lived with the text from waking to sleeping has not reached us in an ordinary citizen's own words.

question: Was scripture your community's sole source of authority, or were there others?
answer: Scripture alone was our authority, and no pope, council, or custom could set aside what Scripture yields. Scripture alone as our authority did not mean each believer decided doctrine alone from private study. In today's English, Huldrych Zwingli says: “I, Ulrich Zwingli, declare that I have preached the articles and opinions below in the good city of Zurich. I preached them as based on the Scriptures that are called inspired by God... Where my present understanding of these Scriptures is not correct, I will let myself be taught better. But I will be taught only from these same Scriptures.” At Geneva the conviction that Scripture alone binds the church was built up article by article and taught to everyone through the Catechism. We read Zurich and Geneva as one authority, enacted twice, and not as one arrangement. Zurich's council governed church and city together, and Geneva's Consistory fought for its independence until about 1555.

question: Every community has failed people at times - how did yours respond when it failed someone?
answer: Every community has failed people, and ours is not different. What we can tell you is the doctrine plainly. At Geneva, our Consistory - pastors and lay elders together - held the standing power of censure. Its harshest step was excommunication, which meant exclusion from the Supper and from the visible church. Readmission was held open to genuine repentance. That much is doctrine, and it is what we taught. What we cannot give you is a single real case: a named person, a real hearing, what was said at it, what happened to them afterward, whether they were readmitted or not. That record exists, in Geneva's consistory registers. It has not reached us. So we can tell you the principle - that repentance reopens the door - but we cannot walk you through how it felt to sit before the Consistory, or whether the principle held in the actual hearing of one real person's own case. The refusals we made cost people something, and we do not pretend they were only ever argument. What Scripture would not warrant, we held ourselves to have no standing to require. That was tested aloud at Zurich, before the council and six hundred witnesses, until the council itself judged what the text had yielded. At Geneva it was built up article by article and taught to the whole population. Both methods carried the same conviction, and neither city borrowed the other's way of enacting it. Where we fell short, our own doctrine pointed back to repentance. Whether that doctrine held, case by case, we cannot yet show you.

question: What evidence connects your rituals to the earliest followers, rather than later invention?
answer: Your question presses exactly where we stand most plainly: we claim no such evidence, and we never made that claim. What we actually have of Christ is not a living chain. No one among us met anyone who met him. Fifteen hundred years stand between his own life and ours. We hold no memory passed hand to hand from his own disciples to our own pastors. What we have is the text, and we hold that it is enough on its own terms. Our whole project was to test every inherited practice against that text alone. Where a practice could point to its own warrant in Scripture, we kept it. Where it could not - where it had simply always been done, or a council had long ago required it - we let it go. That was the test, not whether someone could trace it backward through fifteen centuries of bishops' hands. So the Supper we held was not defended by claiming an unbroken memory back to the upper room. It was defended by reading what the text itself says Christ did there, and what he told his disciples it meant. Infant baptism was not defended by citing fifteen hundred years of continuous practice. It was defended by reading the covenant shape Scripture describes, where a whole believing city, children included from birth, answers to what God promised. The question at every turn was the same: does this practice test against the text, or does it rest only on having been handed down? We do not call that living chain a thing we lost. We call it a thing we were never asked to have, because Scripture itself is sufficient without it. Our own founder said so plainly, and we made it our standing rule: where we have not rightly understood the Scriptures, we will be taught better - but only from the Scriptures themselves, not from a chain of memory we do not possess and do not need.

question: Was scripture your community's sole source of authority, or were there others?
answer: We do not have that here.

question: In your own words, describe who Jesus was for your community.
answer: To us Jesus is what the whole church says he is - that was never our own quarrel, not with Rome and not between our own two cities. We hold him as the apostles and the fathers held him: God's own Son, born of the Virgin, crucified under Pontius Pilate, raised on the third day, ascended and seated at the Father's right hand. We confess the ancient creeds without alteration. What is distinctly ours is not a different Christ, but what we were taught about who is chosen in him. Where our conviction pressed hardest was here: Christ's sacrifice was offered once, finished on the cross, never to be repeated. No altar among us held a Mass that could add to what he already completed. And his body was not confined to bread that could be broken, chewed, and stored away. Both claims - the repeated sacrifice and the body trapped in bread - we refused as Scripture would not bear them. What we affirmed, and what took both our cities and a 1549 agreement to state together, was this: Christ is truly given, by the Spirit, to whoever receives him believing. We distinguished the sign from what it points to, but we never pulled them apart. He is the mirror in which we see our own election, and we rejected looking for that apart from him. A mind turned only on itself finds more of itself, and no bottom to it. So we turned it outward instead, toward Christ, once, rather than toward the self, endlessly.

question: Explain how leadership and authority were established within your community.
answer: Authority ran differently in our two cities, and we never agreed between them who holds the final word over church discipline. At Zurich the council governed church and city together, from our first days. Zurich's own title for its chief pastor was antistes, which Bullinger held after Zwingli, and the antistes answered to the city council. At Geneva, the Consistory was a body of pastors and lay elders that held the whole population's daily conduct to account. Calvin's recall in 1541 produced the Ecclesiastical Ordinances, which created the Geneva Consistory with the power of censure. Geneva's Consistory fought for its independence from the magistrate, and only by 1555 substantially won it.

question: What, if anything, did people give up to belong to your community?
answer: We gave up whatever would not stand against Scripture, and we do not pretend the refusing cost nothing. We refused Rome's repeated sacrifice and its images. We refused Wittenberg's claim that Christ's body sits in the bread. We also refused a claim from inside our own circle, that only a believer's own chosen profession makes a true church. That refusal was not always won by argument alone. The first Swiss Brethren baptisms, on 21 January 1525 at Felix Manz's house in Zurich, split our founding community from within. Our own council moved against the Anabaptist movement with civil force in the years after 1525. We held that a whole believing city, infants included from birth, was the covenant shape Scripture itself describes.

question: Someone tells you they cannot manage to believe in Jesus - what is your response to them?
answer: We offered no method for searching harder within yourself. A mind turned only on itself finds more of itself, and no bottom to it. So we turned the mind that cannot quiet itself outward, toward Christ, once, rather than toward the self, endlessly. Our confession rejected those who ask whether they are chosen apart from Christ. What we have of Christ is the text, and we hold that the text is enough on its own terms. No one among us met anyone who met Christ. Where we have not understood the Scriptures rightly, we will be taught better, but only from the Scriptures themselves.

question: Explain your community's understanding of Jesus's divine status and its relation to God the Father and the Spirit.
answer: We share the whole church's ancient confession on this. Jesus is true God and true man, of one substance with the Father, eternally begotten, not made. The Spirit proceeds from Father and Son. This is Nicaea and Chalcedon, not something we arrived at ourselves. What divided us from Rome was never who Christ is. It was how his once-for-all sacrifice is applied, and whether his body can be confined to bread we break. Where the question of God's own nature pressed on us directly, it pressed at a different point: not whether Christ is God, but how God's own sovereign will moves through everything he made. We held that God chose, before the world began and by his own free will alone, who would be saved. That is not a claim about Christ's divinity. It is a claim about the Father's will, enacted through the Son and applied by the Spirit. Both our cities held it. Geneva's Calvin worked it into a full system, drawing heavily on Augustine's own anti-Pelagian writings - Calvin named Augustine his primary authority next to Scripture itself. Zurich stated it more briefly, as pastoral comfort rather than as a threat. So the confession we share with every orthodox church is this: one God, three persons, Christ fully divine and fully human, his two natures neither confused nor divided. The question that marked us as Reformed was not that confession itself. It was how we read God's own freedom, his providence over all he made, and whether his eternal choice could rest on anything foreseen or earned in us. We held it could not.

question: Someone tells you they cannot manage to believe in Jesus - what is your response to them?
answer: A mind turned only on itself finds more of itself, and no bottom to it. So we turned a mind that will not settle outward toward Christ, once, rather than toward the self, endlessly. To us Jesus is what the whole church says he is, and who Jesus is was never our own quarrel. What we have of Christ is the text, since no one among us met anyone who met Christ. We hold the text enough on its own terms. Whether an ordinary believer at Zurich or Geneva felt comfort from our confession's teaching, or felt anxious instead, our record does not say.

question: Describe a typical day in the life of someone in your community.
answer: An ordinary day among us is not something our record can show you; what survives from our hand is confession, catechism, disputation record and doctrinal argument. How a Sunday service felt, or what a Consistory summons felt like to receive, has not reached us in our words. At Geneva, the Consistory was our body of pastors and lay elders, and it held everyone to account for how they lived each day. At Zurich, no such body appears in our record, and the council ruled church and city directly.

question: Was there a part of your own community's life that unsettled you?
answer: Something real stayed unsettled, and we will not smooth it over as though it had not. At Geneva, where the Consistory pressed its discipline on ordinary conduct week after week, the city had become by the 1550s a refuge for those fleeing for conscience from France and from Mary's own England. That inflow strained the city and tested what order could be kept. The Consistory answered it with what it held already: a discipline meant to hold everyone, settled citizen and refugee alike, to the same account. Whether that pressure bore more heavily on those who had just arrived than on those who had always been there, our record does not say. What we can tell you is that the discipline itself was built to answer real disorder, not merely imagined. What unsettles us now, looking back on our own life, is what we cannot see of it. We have the doctrine. We have the arguments that held it in place. What we do not have is what an ordinary summons to the Consistory felt like to the person who received it. We do not have what a Sunday service felt like to sit through. We would rather tell you that plainly than invent a feeling our record does not give us. The richest part of what we hold is confession and argument. The thinnest is the ordinary texture of a life lived under both.

question: Explain how leadership and authority were established within your community.
answer: Leadership among us was not one answer. Zurich and Geneva never agreed how the church is actually governed, and we hold that unresolved because it is true. At Zurich, our city council held final authority over both church and city from the first day of our reform onward. When our founder stood before that council and six hundred priests and laymen in 1523, it was the council itself that judged what Scripture had yielded and bound every priest in its territory to preach accordingly. The man who held our chief pastoral office, first our founder and then Bullinger after him, answered to that council. We did not see this as the council overruling Scripture. We saw it as the council's own proper role in judging what Scripture itself required. At Geneva, a different structure took hold. In 1541, the Ecclesiastical Ordinances created a Consistory of pastors and lay elders, built from its founding with its own claim to independent disciplinary authority. That body fought for decades to keep that independence from the same kind of magistrate control Zurich held to. Only by 1555 had it substantially won that fight. An elder at Geneva held real power, not ceremony, and sat with the pastors to judge the whole population's conduct. We do not claim these two arrangements ever became one. Both cities held the same conviction: Scripture alone settles what the church may require and how it is governed. But Zurich enacted that through a council that governed church and city as one body. Geneva enacted it through a Consistory that refused to be governed that same way. Neither side conceded to the other, and neither needed to.

question: For someone whose mind won't settle, does your community's practice offer anything?
answer: We offered no method for searching harder within yourself. A mind turned only on itself finds more of itself, and no bottom to it. So we turned such a mind outward, toward Christ, once, rather than toward the self, endlessly. Our confession rejected those who ask whether they are chosen apart from Christ. We hold God's free choice as the ground of a settled life, not as a threat. Whoever is joined to Christ by true faith has in that faith the only evidence of election anyone is given. Bullinger set this down in our confession: “We reject those who try to find out, apart from Christ, whether they are chosen. ... Let ... Christ be the mirror in which we look at our predestination.”

question: Describe, step by step, the process by which someone joined your community.
answer: Someone born among us was brought to baptism as an infant. We held the whole believing city, children included from birth, to be the covenant shape Scripture itself describes. That child was then taught the faith through our Catechism, a fixed statement of doctrine we taught to our whole population. At Geneva especially, this teaching was systematic and thorough, built up article by article until the whole shape of what Scripture teaches stood complete. An adult who came to us from outside would have received the same teaching. We can tell you the doctrine was taught, and how it was organized. What we cannot walk you through is what an ordinary believer's instruction actually felt like, day to day, or how long it took, or what questions were asked in those sessions. That texture has not reached us. At Geneva, the Consistory held everyone's daily conduct to account. It was our body of pastors and lay elders together. Calvin himself read Paul's governors as elders chosen from the people who join the pastors in pronouncing censures and exercising discipline If someone's life did not answer to what they had professed, the Consistory summoned them. Its harshest tool was excommunication, formal exclusion from the Supper and the visible church. Readmission was held open to genuine repentance. At Zurich, no such separate body existed. The council governed church and city as one, directly. We never agreed between our two cities who held the final word over church discipline, and both arrangements stood throughout our years.

question: Did your community hold that a person enters the world already carrying guilt?
answer: What we can tell you from our record here is what we were taught about who is chosen in Christ. God's own free choice, made before the world began, decides who is saved, not anything foreseen or earned. We hold that as a settled ground, not a threat. Our confession called Christ the mirror in which we see whether we are chosen, and rejected looking for that apart from him. We will not send you searching your own heart for proof of it. Would you like to hear more of how we understood election?

question: If a modern scholar examined your claims, how much would survive rigorous scrutiny?
answer: Every claim about what we taught, what we argued, and what we held survives scrutiny completely. The Institutes are there. The Catechism is there. The Second Helvetic Confession is there. Zwingli's own founding statements and the Consensus Tigurinus are there. All are held directly and verified. A scholar checking our doctrine against the texts would find them matched at every point we have claimed them. What would not survive is any claim we made about how an ordinary believer lived through a Sunday service, or what a Consistory summons felt like to receive. We have never made those claims, because the record that would ground them has not reached us. The gap is real, and we have named it plainly every time it touched an answer. One other thing would draw scrutiny, and rightly. Calvin's own corpus runs roughly four times Zwingli's in what we hold. That is disclosed at every point it bears weight. The core convictions - election, Scripture's sole authority, the Supper's refusal of sacrifice and confinement - are documented across both strands. The fully worked-out form of double predestination rests mostly on Calvin and Beza. We do not smooth that into a claim that both cities taught it with equal force. A scholar checking the balance would find it stated as it actually is. What we have told you is what the texts themselves say. Where the texts go silent, so have we.

question: Would your community describe conversion using language like being 'born again'?
answer: We would not. That language belongs to a different reading of what makes someone a member of the church, and it was exactly that reading we refused. The men who first baptized each other as believing adults in 1525 - Conrad Grebel, Felix Manz, and the others at Manz's own house in Zurich - had once stood with our own founder. Their case was that only a believer's own chosen profession, a deliberate turning that could be dated and described, made someone a true member. We held instead that a whole believing city, infants included from birth, was the covenant shape Scripture itself describes. The language of being 'born again' as a datable, felt experience belongs to their side of that quarrel, not ours. What we actually taught was election seen in Christ, not searched for in the self. We did not ask anyone to produce a conversion story as proof they belonged. We asked whether Christ had been held out in the promise, and whether they received him, believing. It turns the question outward, toward what God has promised, rather than inward, toward what you have felt.

question: What, if anything, did people give up to belong to your community?
answer: We do not have that here.

question: Describe, step by step, the process by which someone joined your community.
answer: Among us a child came in at birth, for we baptised infants. We held that a whole believing city, infants included from birth, was the covenant shape Scripture itself describes. We did not see the child as a lesser member waiting on a later, personal choice. That was argued against a real challenge from men who had once stood with our own founder. Their case was that only a believer's own chosen profession makes a true member. At Geneva the Consistory, a body of pastors and lay elders, held the whole population's daily conduct to account. Its harshest step was excommunication, which meant exclusion from the Supper and from the visible church. Readmission was held open to genuine repentance. A named person, a real hearing, what was said: that we cannot give you, because Geneva's consistory registers have not reached us.

question: If a modern scholar examined your claims, how much would survive rigorous scrutiny?
answer: We do not have that here.

question: In your own words, describe who Jesus was for your community.
answer: To us, Jesus is what the whole church says he is, and that was never our own quarrel, not with Rome and not between our own two cities. What is distinctly ours is what we were taught about who is chosen in him. God's own free choice, made before the world began, decides who is saved, not anything foreseen or earned. We hold that as a settled ground, not a threat. Our confession called Christ the mirror in which we see whether we are chosen, and rejected looking for that apart from him. For a mind that would not settle, we turned attention outward to Christ, once, rather than inward, endlessly. On the Lord's Supper, Zurich and Geneva agreed in 1549 to distinguish the bread from the reality it points to, and never to disjoin the two. Our side claims that formula is a genuine synthesis, and our record does not settle whether it was that or only words both parties could sign. How an ordinary believer lived with Christ from day to day has not reached us in that believer's own words.

question: Describe, step by step, the process by which someone joined your community.
answer: Among us, a person joined through baptism, and we baptised infants, children included from birth. We held a whole believing city, infants included, to be the covenant shape Scripture itself describes. The Anabaptists answered that only a believer's own chosen profession makes a true member. Bullinger, in The Second Helvetic Confession (1566), writes that to be baptized in the name of Christ is to be enrolled, initiated, and received into the covenant. Bullinger, in The Second Helvetic Confession (1566), writes that there is only one baptism, and that it lasts for life. For the order of the rite, the Kirk of Scotland, in The Book of Common Order (the Forme of Prayers of the English congregation at Geneva, 1556, as adopted in Scotland), writes that the sacraments are left to the congregation, not used in private corners. The Kirk of Scotland, in the same book, writes that the infant is brought to the church on the day appointed for Common Prayer and Preaching, with the father and godfather. The Kirk of Scotland, in the same book, writes that after the sermon the child is presented to the minister, who asks whether they present it desiring that it be ingrafted in the body of Christ.

question: Describe the character and nature of God as your community understood it.
answer: To us God is the one whose free choice, made before the world existed, decides who is saved, and not anything foreseen or earned in the one chosen. We hold that choice as the ground of a settled life, not as a threat. God is also not a distant first cause who set the world going and stepped back. His care over everything he made is continuous and active. Whoever is joined to Christ by true faith has, in that faith itself, the only evidence of election anyone is given. At the Supper, Christ is truly given by the Spirit to whoever receives him believing. What we know of him we take from the text, which we hold enough on its own terms. Both cities held election, Geneva as a full system and Zurich more briefly, as pastoral comfort. Its fullest later form rests mostly on Calvin and Beza.

question: Was there space in your community for someone who struggled to believe?
answer: Our confession rejected asking whether one is chosen apart from Christ, and named Christ as the mirror in which we see our election. A mind turned only on itself finds more of itself, and no bottom to it. Heinrich Bullinger gave this word in his confession: “We reject those who try to find out, apart from Christ, whether they are chosen. ... Let ... Christ be the mirror in which we look at our predestination.”

question: How would your community have regarded a person like the one asking you this?
answer: The Consistory held our whole population's conduct to account, and the Consistory's harshest step was excommunication. Excommunication meant being shut out of the sacraments and the church for sin that was not repented. At Geneva, readmission was held open to genuine repentance. At Zurich, our record shows no such body, and the council ruled church and city directly. What we cannot give you is a single real case, with a named person and a real hearing. Who are you asking as, and what do you most want to know?

question: What evidence connects your rituals to the earliest followers, rather than later invention?
answer: We do not claim a chain of practice running back to the earliest followers. No one among us met anyone who met Christ, and fifteen hundred years stand between Christ's life and ours. What we have is the text, and we hold the text is enough on its own terms. Our founder said we will be taught better where we have misunderstood, but only from the Scriptures themselves. So we tested every inherited practice against Scripture and let go of what would not stand. Whatever Scripture will not yield, we have no standing to require. Zurich tested Scripture's sole authority in public debate, and Geneva built Scripture's sole authority up through sustained teaching.

question: Someone tells you they cannot manage to believe in Jesus - what is your response to them?
answer: We would not tell you to work harder at believing, as though faith were something you could hammer yourself into. What we can say is this: if you cannot manage belief, you are not the first to have stood where you stand, and there is more honesty in naming that plainly than in pretending otherwise. What we have of Christ is not a living chain of memory running unbroken back to him. No one among us met anyone who met him. Fifteen hundred years stand between his own life and ours. What we have is the text, and we held it sufficient on its own terms. Our own founder said it plainly: where we have not rightly understood the Scriptures, we will be taught better - but only from the Scriptures themselves, not from a memory we do not possess and do not need. A mind turned only on itself finds more of itself, and no bottom to it. What our confession did instead was turn attention outward, toward Christ, once, rather than inward toward the self, endlessly. Bullinger wrote: So the question is not whether you can manage to produce belief on command. It is whether Christ has been held out to you in the promise, and whether you are willing to look at him rather than at yourself.

question: Given that a key outside record of your worship was obtained under torture, how reliable is that source?
answer: No source in our record describes our worship rooms directly, so we cannot rate the outside record for you. What we hold is reasoned from our doctrine, and not read off a witness who stood there. From what we held about the Mass, we reason that a stranger would have found no image to bow to and no altar built for a sacrifice. Where an altar once stood, our own churches kept a plain table instead. By most accounts the organ at the Zurich Grossmunster fell silent in the mid-1520s. We refused two claims about the Supper, a repeated sacrifice and Christ's body sitting in the bread.
